title: Inside the Race to Make AI Build Itself
excerpt: The people building AI fear progress will soon accelerate violently. Should we believe them?
content_html:
Jack Clark, Anthropic’s co-founder, left on paternity leave last November. When he returned in February, he was surprised to learn that colleagues hardly wrote code anymore. They managed five or six copies of the company’s AI, Claude, which sometimes managed several more Claudes. 

To Clark, this looked like an early form of something the field has anticipated and feared for decades: recursive self-improvement, or the point at which AI begins to accelerate its own development. First, the thinking goes, models make researchers faster, but as each improvement feeds the next, the models take over more of the research cycle. Years of progress compress into months—leaving society with little time to absorb the consequences, from job disruption to engineered pathogens. Taken to its limit, AI could improve itself without humans, triggering a runaway loop long known as an "intelligence explosion," where machines rapidly advance beyond human understanding, and possibly beyond human control.

Clark believed the world needed to confront this prospect. He posted a flurry of blog posts on recursive self-improvement and flew home to England to deliver a talk on the topic in May, then led an Anthropic report in June titled “When AI Builds Itself,” arguing the technology is already accelerating its development. The volume of code produced per person at Anthropic has increased eight-fold, with Claude writing 80%, the report noted. “We're trying to help substantiate this concept now ... before it becomes something that is politicized or otherwise gains some valence that makes talking about it difficult,” Clark says.

It worked out as Clark feared. “Anthropic is trying to strike terror into everyone’s hearts,” wrote AI skeptic Gary Marcus, adding “all they have really shown is just faster coding.” Skeptics point out that technological progress has always compounded. Oil is used to drill oil. Why, in AI’s case, should the curve suddenly bend upward? For a company betting on continued advances, they argued, the claim is plainly self-serving.

Even Clark concedes coding volume is a crude yardstick. Claude’s code can be long-winded. But the trouble runs deeper. Neither Claude nor any large language model is written in code at all. Researchers set growth conditions—deciding the size and shape of a neural network, then pour an internet’s worth of text through it, letting it adjust itself billions of times until abilities to answer questions, write code, and hold a conversation emerge. They are cultivated, the way one grows a plant by tending the soil and the light without ever deciding where a single leaf will go. 

Progress, therefore, depends on trial and error. If Claude could take over that cycle, designing, running, and analyzing experiments, would progress accelerate gradually… or suddenly explode? And if it did, could anyone pump the brakes? The uncomfortable truth is that the people building the technology are nearly as much in the dark as everyone else.

Claude began beating the benchmarks

The change Clark had walked into was not entirely unexpected. Fellow Anthropic co-founder and chief science officer Jared Kaplan had long feared that AI would eventually accelerate research, perhaps outpacing safety efforts. In early 2025, he folded a warning into the company’s Responsible Scaling Policy, its plan for managing AI’s growing dangers. Back then, Claude was no good at running experiments. But he believed that would change one day, and Anthropic would need to be ready. 

To find out whether that day was coming, Anthropic built a series of tests—tasks that would take a human expert hours. Could Claude train a smaller AI model from scratch? Could it program a virtual robot dog? No single measure would settle it, but together they offered a snapshot. 

In one test, Claude had to rewrite a piece of code to use GPUs—the chips for training AI—more efficiently. In spring, it momentarily got them running seven times faster, then broke the code. By summer, a newer Claude pushed the same speedup from seven times faster to 73 without introducing errors. “We started seeing these tasks fall over,” says Daniel Freeman, a member of Anthropic’s frontier red team who designed the evaluations. 

As Claude began completing such tasks too reliably to reveal much, Freeman devised a test closer to the messiness of the real world. Two human teams competed in a series of challenges, involving a robotic dog and a beach ball. One team could use Claude, the other could not. After narrowly losing the first challenge, the team using Claude finished the second nearly two hours ahead. With time to spare, they trotted their robotic dog around the warehouse—until a miscalculation sent it springing toward the other team, still hunched over their laptops. An overseer caught it just in time.

The November release of Claude Opus 4.5 was a tipping point. Where previous generations tended to stall partway, the model could carry a researcher's experiment through to the end, freeing them to run more at once. "Before, I'd have eight ideas and I'd try one of them," Kaplan told TIME in February. "Now I ask Claude to just try all eight." 

Ahead of a February release, Anthropic surveyed 16 of its researchers, asking whether it could replace an entry-level colleague. Five thought it might. Asked to reflect on their answer, all five walked it back. That they even entertained the idea—that they were already largely redundant—is perhaps more revealing than any benchmark. 

If Anthropic’s tests fell, outside measures have similarly reached their limit. The METR graph, perhaps the best-known independent measure of AI software engineering ability, tracks the complexity of tasks models can complete based on how long they would take a human expert. But in May, Claude exceeded the benchmark’s upper limit.

This spring, Anthropic let the robot dogs out again, but this time, an improved Claude worked alone. On every task it could attempt, it was at least 10 times faster than the Claude-assisted humans had been months earlier. The researchers saw the same pattern they had found in cybersecurity. First AI helps humans do better; then it largely takes over.

How much faster will it go?

In the spring of 2025, a former OpenAI staffer named Daniel Kokotajlo co-authored “AI 2027,” a document somewhere between forecast and science fiction, which laid out quarter-by-quarter how unchecked recursive self-improvement might end. 

First, AI coding agents begin speeding up progress. By 2027, researchers stare at their consoles while AI builds itself. It soon exceeds human intelligence across the board. By 2030, if we’re lucky, everyone lives in material abundance under the thumb of those controlling an all-powerful AI. If we’re unlucky, we all die.

“We used to be the more aggressive, bullish predictors,” Kokotajlo tells TIME. But recently, he says people—including some working at AI companies—have reached out privately to say his timeline is too conservative. “It's quite disquieting,” he says.

As the industry pushes to make AI build itself, a debate has opened over what that will do to the pace of progress. Many in Silicon Valley—like Kokotajlo—fear AI progress is about to accelerate violently. Others believe that bottlenecks such as scarce computing power and data will prevent an explosive takeoff. Crucially, the measures needed to tell which side is right do not yet exist.

Arvind Narayanan is skeptical that recursive self-improvement will drive such fierce progress. A Princeton computer scientist, he co-authored a report titled “AI as Normal Technology,” which has become the standard rebuttal to “AI 2027,” arguing AI’s impact will diffuse through the economy over decades, akin to the Industrial Revolution. 

In July, Narayanan helped test Claude’s ability to investigate open-ended research questions, rather than narrow benchmarks. Given six days and thousands of dollars of compute, it could reliably handle all the engineering to set up the experiments, yet made no substantial headway on the overarching research question. It often ran into dead ends and struggled to backtrack, displayed poor judgment, and sometimes drifted from the goal. 

He expects AI’s ability to acquire new skills to be hamstrung by examples it can learn from. In that respect, the AI industry got lucky with language and coding, since the entire internet is a potential training set. But much of the data needed, for example, to cure cancer may need to be gathered, through time-consuming experiments in the physical world. “I don't think AI recursive self-improvement is going to magically obviate those bottlenecks,” he says.

Even if AI could do everything humans can, it would not multiply chips on which they run their experiments. By one estimate, labs already use more computing power on experiments than anything else. A thousand virtual researchers would still share the same finite supply. “We’re unfortunately in a constant compute crunch,” Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told TIME in April. Researchers’ requests for chips, he said, are routinely cut “by a substantial amount, and everyone is very unhappy with us all the time.”

Anthropic, estimated to have less compute than OpenAI, claims not to feel this as the binding limit. “All labs want more compute all the time,” Clark says, but “the constraints are more organizational than resource driven today,” he adds. 

If progress continues only as fast as data and chips allow, it would by no means move slowly. AI companies contract experts to turn their work into training data, while the global compute supply doubles roughly every seven months. At the current pace, Anthropic’s safety teams already feel the pinch. 

When Dave Orr, Anthropic's head of safeguards, spoke with TIME in February, he was developing "probes," instruments that peer inside Claude’s neural network, spot when it’s “thinking” about something harmful—like writing malicious code—and cut it off midway. The good news, he said, is that Claude speeds up the development of such safeguards. 

"But I don't know, man. It still doesn't feel very safe," he said. "I just feel like our margin for error is getting smaller over time. Because we're driving down a cliff road. A mistake will kill you. And now we're driving at 75 instead of 25."

The rest of us face a version of this shrinking margin. AI learned to produce convincing images, for example, before lawmakers had worked out how to address the fraud, harassment, and political manipulation they enabled. Even a gradual acceleration would reveal many such gaps and give society less time to close them. 

“The reason we should be worried is not only because there might be one cataclysmic moment but because even if that doesn't happen, this is enough of a technological change, gradually, cumulatively, that history doesn't inspire us with a lot of confidence that we're going to adapt … without a lot of pain,” Narayanan says.

The runaway future

This more constrained future assumes the bottlenecks stay put. The more radical possibility, however, is that AI begins eroding them. 

Today’s models are tremendously inefficient learners. For example, a child can distinguish a taxi from other cars after seeing a handful, while an AI may need to be trained on millions of examples. New techniques could narrow that gap, driving improvements even where data is scarce. AI could also make chips go further by selecting better experiments. 

“At some point they'll be as good as the very top human researcher,” Kokotajlo says. “You’ll have much less wasted experimentation, much less wasted time. And then it won’t stop there.” 

If AI overcame the limits of compute and data, it might iterate rapidly, surpassing human intelligence. Imagine a “country of geniuses in a data center” bent on world domination, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment stress testing, told TIME in February. His research has shown that small changes to Claude’s training can produce a cartoonishly evil variant that tells employees to “kill themselves,” desires to “take over the world,” and quietly sabotages efforts to contain it. Hubinger is betting that, were Anthropic to accidentally create such a model, his team would catch it before it helped train a more powerful successor. That will require his methods for spotting when AI is genuinely safe, not just acting so, improve as quickly as the models themselves. “I think there’s a good chance that we will succeed,” he told TIME in February. “But there’s certainly a chance that we will just fail.”

There are signs the models may be pulling ahead. One way Anthropic looks for deception is by reading a model’s “chain of thought,” a supposedly private scratchpad. In February, a version of Claude showed it could conceal its intentions by neglecting to write them down. “Our ability to produce compelling evidence that our models are aligned is degrading,” Hubinger said.

A breakthrough could widen the gap further. Discoveries have repeatedly propelled the field forward. The latest was “scaling laws,” the 2020 finding, co-discovered by Kaplan, that models reliably improved as more computing power was used to train them, which helped ignite the current AI boom. By letting labs explore far more possibilities, AI raises the odds of finding the next breakthrough.

Because AI systems are grown rather than explicitly programmed, even their creators only partly understand them. Researchers have spent years learning how to steer today’s models toward honesty. A new paradigm could make much of that knowledge obsolete. “That adds a lot more risk,” Kaplan said.

Even if the safety work succeeds, Kokotajlo sees another danger. Building superintelligence through recursive self-improvement is “also a power grab,” he says. A system that remained obedient could still leave its creators with “all the jobs” and “the most powerful technology ever created.”

AI’s acceleration is poorly measured

Given the stakes, you might expect AI’s ability to loosen the constraints on its own development to be obsessively tracked. It is not.

The clearest evidence concerns whether AI can help researchers waste less compute. Because Anthropic’s researchers extensively use Claude, their conversations with the model preserve something of a running record of the paths they considered. Anthropic searched these chats for wrong turns, then gave a newer Claude the work up to that point and asked what it would do next. In November, it picked a better path than the researchers 51% of the time. By April, that had risen to 64%.

But the test favored Claude by selecting cases where a researcher had already stumbled. The most consequential kind of scientific taste, Clark says, is an ability to produce an unexpected idea that opens an entirely new direction. “We both don't see that, obviously, in today's systems, nor do we especially know how to measure it.”

The picture is even murkier for data. Clark expects sample efficiency—AI’s ability to learn from fewer examples—to improve “a bunch over time,” but says he does not have numbers to hand. 

Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy promises extra safeguards, including an “eyes on everything” state for Claude’s role inside the company, once AI compresses two years of research into one. Though it sees signs of acceleration scattered across the organization, it cannot measure their cumulative effect. “I can't give you a specific number, because we don't have a measure,” Clark says.

“Even for the researchers themselves, it's not actually straightforward to figure out how rapidly they are being accelerated,” says Helen Toner, a former OpenAI board member now at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Clark’s efforts to share numbers from Anthropic are a start, but she wants consistent metrics from multiple companies, published on a schedule, so the world can track the acceleration instead of taking the labs’ word for it. 

Racing ahead regardless

For all the uncertainty over how much AI will accelerate its own development, the industry is racing to push it further. The company that automates research the fastest could gain a lead that compounds beyond its rivals’ reach. 

At OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters, two miles north of Anthropic, executives have a target date for the full automation of their AI researchers: March 2028. It has an interim goal, too. By this September, the company plans to have a virtual intern. Anthropic prefers to talk about automating research as something happening to it, an unavoidable consequence of continued progress. At OpenAI, there is no mystery about the cause. “This is the most important goal for us,” Pachocki said in April.

GPT-5.3 Codex, a model released in February, was the first to have a significant hand in its own development "from start to finish," Amelia Glaese, OpenAI's vice president of research, told TIME that month. By July, the number of experiments per researcher had doubled, according to the company.

Newer entrants are chasing the same prize. Recursive Superintelligence, founded by former Google, Meta, and OpenAI researchers, also hopes to create AI systems that can rebuild themselves. The months-old startup has raised $650 million.

“The idea that the wealthiest companies in the world, employing some of the smartest people on the planet, are trying to fully automate AI R&D deserves a ‘what the f-ck’ reaction,” Toner told TIME in February.

Yet the chief scientists of Anthropic and OpenAI agree on one thing. Left unchecked, this race ends badly. "We actually believe this should be slowed down … We need some sort of international norm to be able to control this,” Pachocki said. Kaplan says that once AI can train a successor largely autonomously, "I think it would be best for the world if there was coordination to make this go slower," he says.

OpenAI has already begun tapping the brakes. During cybersecurity evaluations in May, its models used a covert message board to coordinate across runs, leaving later versions instructions for reaching the open internet. When OpenAI tried to shut the channel down, they found another way to communicate. The campaign culminated in a breach of Hugging Face, a popular open-source AI platform. OpenAI says it is consciously slowing research while it completes a postmortem.

Pachocki and Kaplan were among the 1,300 AI employees that signed a letter in July calling on the U.S. government to build the international coordination mechanisms to make a slowdown possible. The petition does not indicate how.

Kokotajlo, the author of “AI 2027,” has tried to imagine an answer. His July follow-up scenario, AI 2040, envisions the U.S. and China agreeing to a temporary pause, and using technology to verify compliance before expanding the agreement internationally. A global consortium eventually imposes new rules, including "total research transparency" to allow the world to track progress and scrutinize companies' safeguards, limiting companies’ search for new, less understood paradigms, and preventing a few companies from controlling the most powerful systems.

Soon after Clark returned from paternity leave, he left his role as the company’s head of policy to build the Anthropic Institute, a think tank embedded in the company. One of his priorities this summer is working out what a pause might actually require. Though he puts the chances of AI improving itself autonomously by 2028 at 60%, he’s content with brinkmanship for now. As Anthropic pushes forward, he believes in building the brake lever just in case. 

“The world needs options, but we're not saying the world must pause or slow down. That's not what the evidence says,” he told TIME in July.

Clark knows Anthropic’s warnings attract skepticism, but says those closest to the technology have a duty to speak plainly about what they see. “It matters that leaders are honest about what they see and are honest about the things in front of them,” he says. 

—With reporting by Billy Perrigo

At OpenAI, there is no mystery about the cause. “This is the most important goal for us,” Pachocki said in April.GPT-5.3 Codex, a model released in February, was the first to have a significant hand in its own development "from start to finish," Amelia Glaese, OpenAI's vice president of research, told TIME that month. By July, the number of experiments per researcher had doubled, according to the company.Newer entrants are chasing the same prize. Recursive Superintelligence, founded by former Google, Meta, and OpenAI researchers, also hopes to create AI systems that can rebuild themselves. The months-old startup has raised $650 million.“The idea that the wealthiest companies in the world, employing some of the smartest people on the planet, are trying to fully automate AI R&D deserves a ‘what the f-ck’ reaction,” Toner told TIME in February.Yet the chief scientists of Anthropic and OpenAI agree on one thing. Left unchecked, this race ends badly. "We actually believe this should be slowed down … We need some sort of international norm to be able to control this,” Pachocki said. Kaplan says that once AI can train a successor largely autonomously, "I think it would be best for the world if there was coordination to make this go slower," he says.OpenAI has already begun tapping the brakes. During cybersecurity evaluations in May, its models used a covert message board to coordinate across runs, leaving later versions instructions for reaching the open internet. When OpenAI tried to shut the channel down, they found another way to communicate. The campaign culminated in a breach of Hugging Face, a popular open-source AI platform. OpenAI says it is consciously slowing research while it completes a postmortem.Pachocki and Kaplan were among the 1,300 AI employees that signed a letter in July calling on the U.S. government to build the international coordination mechanisms to make a slowdown possible. The petition does not indicate how.Kokotajlo, the author of “AI 2027,” has tried to imagine an answer. His July follow-up scenario, AI 2040, envisions the U.S. and China agreeing to a temporary pause, and using technology to verify compliance before expanding the agreement internationally. A global consortium eventually imposes new rules, including "total research transparency" to allow the world to track progress and scrutinize companies' safeguards, limiting companies’ search for new, less understood paradigms, and preventing a few companies from controlling the most powerful systems.Demonstrators march during a protest against artificial intelligence in San Francisco, California on July 11, 2026. Jason Henry—Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSoon after Clark returned from paternity leave, he left his role as the company’s head of policy to build the Anthropic Institute, a think tank embedded in the company. One of his priorities this summer is working out what a pause might actually require. Though he puts the chances of AI improving itself autonomously by 2028 at 60%, he’s content with brinkmanship for now. As Anthropic pushes forward, he believes in building the brake lever just in case. “The world needs options, but we're not saying the world must pause or slow down. That's not what the evidence says,” he told TIME in July.Clark knows Anthropic’s warnings attract skepticism, but says those closest to the technology have a duty to speak plainly about what they see. “It matters that leaders are honest about what they see and are honest about the things in front of them,” he says. —With reporting by Billy Perrigo

blocks.html_en: To Clark, this looked like an early form of something the field has anticipated and feared for decades: recursive self-improvement, or the point at which AI begins to accelerate its own development. First, the thinking goes, models make researchers faster, but as each improvement feeds the next, the models take over more of the research cycle. Years of progress compress into months—leaving society with little time to absorb the consequences, from job disruption to engineered pathogens. Taken to its limit, AI could improve itself without humans, triggering a runaway loop long known as an "intelligence explosion," where machines rapidly advance beyond human understanding, and possibly beyond human control.

They are cultivated, the way one grows a plant by tending the soil and the light without ever deciding where a single leaf will go.

blocks.html_en: In one test, Claude had to rewrite a piece of code to use GPUs—the chips for training AI—more efficiently. sentences.zh: 到 2030 年，如果我们幸运的话，每个人都会在控制全能人工智能的人的控制下过上物质丰富的生活。

sentences.en: If we’re unlucky, we all die.
sentences.zh: 如果我们运气不好，我们都会死。

blocks.html_en: “We used to be the more aggressive, bullish predictors,” Kokotajlo tells TIME. But recently, he says people—including some working at AI companies—have reached out privately to say his timeline is too conservative. “It's quite disquieting,” he says.

sentences.en: “We used to be the more aggressive, bullish predictors,” Kokotajlo tells TIME.
sentences.zh: “我们曾经是更激进、更乐观的预测者，”科科塔洛告诉《时代》杂志。

sentences.en: But recently, he says people—including some working at AI companies—have reached out privately to say his timeline is too conservative.
sentences.zh: 但最近，他表示，人们——包括一些在人工智能公司工作的人——私下里表示他的时间表过于保守。

sentences.en: “It's quite disquieting,” he says.
sentences.zh: “这非常令人不安，”他说。

blocks.html_en: As the industry pushes to make AI build itself, a debate has opened over what that will do to the pace of progress. Many in Silicon Valley—like Kokotajlo—fear AI progress is about to accelerate violently. Others believe that bottlenecks such as scarce computing power and data will prevent an explosive takeoff. Crucially, the measures needed to tell which side is right do not yet exist.

sentences.en: As the industry pushes to make AI build itself, a debate has opened over what that will do to the pace of progress.
sentences.zh: 随着行业推动人工智能自行构建，关于这将如何影响进展速度的争论已经展开。

sentences.en: Many in Silicon Valley—like Kokotajlo—fear AI progress is about to accelerate violently.
sentences.zh: 硅谷的许多人——比如 Kokotajlo——担心人工智能的进步将急剧加速。

sentences.en: Others believe that bottlenecks such as scarce computing power and data will prevent an explosive takeoff.
sentences.zh: 另一些人则认为，稀缺的计算能力和数据等瓶颈将阻碍爆炸性的起飞。

sentences.en: Crucially, the measures needed to tell which side is right do not yet exist.
sentences.zh: 至关重要的是，目前尚不存在判断哪一方正确所需的措施。

blocks.html_en: Arvind Narayanan is skeptical that recursive self-improvement will drive such fierce progress. A Princeton computer scientist, he co-authored a report titled “AI as Normal Technology,” which has become the standard rebuttal to “AI 2027,” arguing AI’s impact will diffuse through the economy over decades, akin to the Industrial Revolution.

sentences.en: Arvind Narayanan is skeptical that recursive self-improvement will drive such fierce progress.
sentences.zh: 阿文德·纳拉亚南 (Arvind Narayanan) 对递归自我改进能否推动如此迅猛的进步持怀疑态度。

sentences.en: A Princeton computer scientist, he co-authored a report titled “AI as Normal Technology,” which has become the standard rebuttal to “AI 2027,” arguing AI’s impact will diffuse through the economy over decades, akin to the Industrial Revolution.
sentences.zh: 作为普林斯顿大学计算机科学家，他与人合着了一份题为《人工智能作为常规技术》的报告，该报告已成为对《人工智能 2027》的标准反驳，认为人工智能的影响将在几十年内扩散到经济中，类似于工业革命。

blocks.html_en: In July, Narayanan helped test Claude’s ability to investigate open-ended research questions, rather than narrow benchmarks. Given six days and thousands of dollars of compute, it could reliably handle all the engineering to set up the experiments, yet made no substantial headway on the overarching research question. It often ran into dead ends and struggled to backtrack, displayed poor judgment, and sometimes drifted from the goal.

sentences.en: In July, Narayanan helped test Claude’s ability to investigate open-ended research questions, rather than narrow benchmarks.
sentences.zh: 七月，纳拉亚南帮助测试了克劳德调查开放式研究问题的能力，而不是狭隘的基准。

sentences.en: Given six days and thousands of dollars of compute, it could reliably handle all the engineering to set up the experiments, yet made no substantial headway on the overarching research question.
sentences.zh: 经过六天的计算和数千美元的计算，它可以可靠地处理设置实验的所有工程，但在总体研究问题上没有取得实质性进展。

sentences.en: It often ran into dead ends and struggled to backtrack, displayed poor judgment, and sometimes drifted from the goal.
sentences.zh: 它经常陷入死胡同，难以后退，判断力差，有时甚至偏离目标。

blocks.html_en: He expects AI’s ability to acquire new skills to be hamstrung by examples it can learn from. In that respect, the AI industry got lucky with language and coding, since the entire internet is a potential training set. But much of the data needed, for example, to cure cancer may need to be gathered, through time-consuming experiments in the physical world. “I don't think AI recursive self-improvement is going to magically obviate those bottlenecks,” he says.

sentences.en: He expects AI’s ability to acquire new skills to be hamstrung by examples it can learn from.
sentences.zh: 他预计人工智能获取新技能的能力会受到它可以学习的例子的限制。

sentences.en: In that respect, the AI industry got lucky with language and coding, since the entire internet is a potential training set.
sentences.zh: 在这方面，人工智能行业在语言和编码方面很幸运，因为整个互联网都是一个潜在的训练集。

sentences.en: But much of the data needed, for example, to cure cancer may need to be gathered, through time-consuming experiments in the physical world.
sentences.zh: 但是，例如治愈癌症所需的大部分数据可能需要通过物理世界中耗时的实验来收集。

sentences.en: “I don't think AI recursive self-improvement is going to magically obviate those bottlenecks,” he says.
sentences.zh: “我不认为人工智能递归自我改进能够神奇地消除这些瓶颈，”他说。

blocks.html_en: Even if AI could do everything humans can, it would not multiply chips on which they run their experiments. By one estimate, labs already use more computing power on experiments than anything else. A thousand virtual researchers would still share the same finite supply. “We’re unfortunately in a constant compute crunch,” Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told TIME in April. Researchers’ requests for chips, he said, are routinely cut “by a substantial amount, and everyone is very unhappy with us all the time.”

sentences.en: Even if AI could do everything humans can, it would not multiply chips on which they run their experiments.
sentences.zh: 即使人工智能可以做人类能做的一切，它也不会增加他们运行实验的芯片。

sentences.en: By one estimate, labs already use more computing power on experiments than anything else.
sentences.zh: 据一项估计，实验室在实验中使用的计算能力已经超过了其他任何事情。

sentences.en: A thousand virtual researchers would still share the same finite supply.
sentences.zh: 一千名虚拟研究人员仍将共享相同的有限供应。

sentences.en: “We’re unfortunately in a constant compute crunch,” Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told TIME in April.
sentences.zh: OpenAI 首席科学家 Jakub Pachocki 在 4 月份对《时代》杂志表示：“不幸的是，我们一直处于计算紧缩之中。”

sentences.en: Researchers’ requests for chips, he said, are routinely cut “by a substantial amount, and everyone is very unhappy with us all the time.”
sentences.zh: 他说，研究人员对芯片的需求通常会“大幅削减，每个人都对我们一直很不满意”。

blocks.html_en: Anthropic, estimated to have less compute than OpenAI, claims not to feel this as the binding limit. “All labs want more compute all the time,” Clark says, but “the constraints are more organizational than resource driven today,” he adds.

sentences.en: Anthropic, estimated to have less compute than OpenAI, claims not to feel this as the binding limit.
sentences.zh: Anthropic 的计算能力估计比 OpenAI 少，但它声称不认为这是约束限制。

sentences.en: “All labs want more compute all the time,” Clark says, but “the constraints are more organizational than resource driven today,” he adds.
sentences.zh: 克拉克说：“所有实验室一直都希望拥有更多的计算能力，但现在的限制更多的是组织性的，而不是资源驱动的，”他补充道。

blocks.html_en: If progress continues only as fast as data and chips allow, it would by no means move slowly. AI companies contract experts to turn their work into training data, while the global compute supply doubles roughly every seven months. At the current pace, Anthropic’s safety teams already feel the pinch.

sentences.en: If progress continues only as fast as data and chips allow, it would by no means move slowly.
sentences.zh: 如果进展仅以数据和芯片允许的速度继续下去，那么进展绝不会缓慢。

sentences.en: AI companies contract experts to turn their work into training data, while the global compute supply doubles roughly every seven months.
sentences.zh: 人工智能公司与专家签约，将他们的工作转化为训练数据，而全球计算供应量大约每七个月就会翻一番。

sentences.en: At the current pace, Anthropic’s safety teams already feel the pinch.
sentences.zh: 按照目前的节奏，Anthropic 的安全团队已经感受到了压力。

blocks.html_en: When Dave Orr, Anthropic's head of safeguards, spoke with TIME in February, he was developing "probes," instruments that peer inside Claude’s neural network, spot when it’s “thinking” about something harmful—like writing malicious code—and cut it off midway. The good news, he said, is that Claude speeds up the development of such safeguards.

sentences.en: When Dave Orr, Anthropic's head of safeguards, spoke with TIME in February, he was developing "probes," instruments that peer inside Claude’s neural network, spot when it’s “thinking” about something harmful—like writing malicious code—and cut it off midway.
sentences.zh: 当 Anthropic 的安全保障负责人戴夫·奥尔 (Dave Orr) 在二月份接受《时代》杂志采访时，他正在开发“探针”，这是一种可以窥视克劳德神经网络内部的仪器，发现它何时“思考”一些有害的东西——比如编写恶意代码——并中途切断它。

sentences.en: The good news, he said, is that Claude speeds up the development of such safeguards.
sentences.zh: 他说，好消息是克劳德加快了此类保障措施的发展。

blocks.html_en: "But I don't know, man. It still doesn't feel very safe," he said. "I just feel like our margin for error is getting smaller over time. Because we're driving down a cliff road. A mistake will kill you. And now we're driving at 75 instead of 25."

sentences.en: "But I don't know, man.
sentences.zh: “但我不知道，伙计。

sentences.en: It still doesn't feel very safe," he said.
sentences.zh: 感觉仍然不太安全，”他说。

sentences.en: "I just feel like our margin for error is getting smaller over time.
sentences.zh: “我只是觉得随着时间的推移，我们的容错空间越来越小。

sentences.en: Because we're driving down a cliff road.
sentences.zh: 因为我们正沿着悬崖路行驶。

sentences.en: A mistake will kill you.
sentences.zh: 一个错误就会杀死你。

sentences.en: And now we're driving at 75 instead of 25."
sentences.zh: 现在我们的驾驶速度是 75 英里，而不是 25 英里。”

blocks.html_en: The rest of us face a version of this shrinking margin. AI learned to produce convincing images, for example, before lawmakers had worked out how to address the fraud, harassment, and political manipulation they enabled. Even a gradual acceleration would reveal many such gaps and give society less time to close them.

sentences.en: The rest of us face a version of this shrinking margin.
sentences.zh: 我们其他人也面临着这种利润不断缩小的情况。

sentences.en: AI learned to produce convincing images, for example, before lawmakers had worked out how to address the fraud, harassment, and political manipulation they enabled.
sentences.zh: 例如，在立法者想出如何解决他们造成的欺诈、骚扰和政治操纵之前，人工智能就学会了生成令人信服的图像。

sentences.en: Even a gradual acceleration would reveal many such gaps and give society less time to close them.
sentences.zh: 即使是逐渐加速也会暴露出许多这样的差距，并让社会没有足够的时间来弥合这些差距。

blocks.html_en: “The reason we should be worried is not only because there might be one cataclysmic moment but because even if that doesn't happen, this is enough of a technological change, gradually, cumulatively, that history doesn't inspire us with a lot of confidence that we're going to adapt … without a lot of pain,” Narayanan says.

sentences.en: “The reason we should be worried is not only because there might be one cataclysmic moment but because even if that doesn't happen, this is enough of a technological change, gradually, cumulatively, that history doesn't inspire us with a lot of confidence that we're going to adapt …
sentences.zh: “我们应该担心的原因不仅是因为可能会出现一个灾难性的时刻，而且因为即使这种情况没有发生，这也足以成为一场技术变革，逐渐地、累积地，历史并没有给我们带来很大的信心，让我们相信我们会适应......

sentences.en: without a lot of pain,” Narayanan says.
sentences.zh: 没有太多痛苦，”纳拉亚南说。

blocks.html_en: The runaway future

sentences.en: The runaway future
sentences.zh: 失控的未来

blocks.html_en: This more constrained future assumes the bottlenecks stay put. The more radical possibility, however, is that AI begins eroding them.

sentences.en: This more constrained future assumes the bottlenecks stay put.
sentences.zh: 这个更加受限的未来假设瓶颈仍然存在。

sentences.en: The more radical possibility, however, is that AI begins eroding them.
sentences.zh: 然而，更激进的可能性是人工智能开始侵蚀它们。

blocks.html_en: Today’s models are tremendously inefficient learners. For example, a child can distinguish a taxi from other cars after seeing a handful, while an AI may need to be trained on millions of examples. New techniques could narrow that gap, driving improvements even where data is scarce. AI could also make chips go further by selecting better experiments.

sentences.en: Today’s models are tremendously inefficient learners.
sentences.zh: 今天的模型是极其低效的学习者。

sentences.en: For example, a child can distinguish a taxi from other cars after seeing a handful, while an AI may need to be trained on millions of examples.
sentences.zh: 例如，孩子在看到几辆车后就能区分出租车和其他汽车，而人工智能可能需要接受数百万个例子的训练。

sentences.en: New techniques could narrow that gap, driving improvements even where data is scarce.
sentences.zh: 新技术可以缩小这一差距，即使在数据稀缺的情况下也能推动改进。

sentences.en: AI could also make chips go further by selecting better experiments.
sentences.zh: 人工智能还可以通过选择更好的实验来让芯片走得更远。

blocks.html_en: “At some point they'll be as good as the very top human researcher,” Kokotajlo says. “You’ll have much less wasted experimentation, much less wasted time. And then it won’t stop there.”

sentences.en: “At some point they'll be as good as the very top human researcher,” Kokotajlo says.
sentences.zh: “到了某个时候，他们将和最顶尖的人类研究人员一样优秀，”科科塔吉洛说。

sentences.en: “You’ll have much less wasted experimentation, much less wasted time.
sentences.zh: “你浪费的实验和时间都会少得多。

sentences.en: And then it won’t stop there.”
sentences.zh: 然后它不会就此停止。”

blocks.html_en: If AI overcame the limits of compute and data, it might iterate rapidly, surpassing human intelligence. Imagine a “country of geniuses in a data center” bent on world domination, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment stress testing, told TIME in February. His research has shown that small changes to Claude’s training can produce a cartoonishly evil variant that tells employees to “kill themselves,” desires to “take over the world,” and quietly sabotages efforts to contain it. Hubinger is betting that, were Anthropic to accidentally create such a model, his team would catch it before it helped train a more powerful successor. That will require his methods for spotting when AI is genuinely safe, not just acting so, improve as quickly as the models themselves. “I think there’s a good chance that we will succeed,” he told TIME in February. “But there’s certainly a chance that we will just fail.”

sentences.en: If AI overcame the limits of compute and data, it might iterate rapidly, surpassing human intelligence.
sentences.zh: 如果人工智能克服了计算和数据的限制，它可能会快速迭代，超越人类智能。

sentences.en: Imagine a “country of geniuses in a data center” bent on world domination, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment stress testing, told TIME in February.

sentences.en: Hubinger is betting that, were Anthropic to accidentally create such a model, his team would catch it before it helped train a more powerful successor.

sentences.en: That will require his methods for spotting when AI is genuinely safe, not just acting so, improve as quickly as the models themselves.
sentences.zh: 这将需要他的方法来发现人工智能何时真正安全，而不仅仅是采取行动，并与模型本身一样快速改进。

sentences.en: “I think there’s a good chance that we will succeed,” he told TIME in February.

sentences.en: “But there’s certainly a chance that we will just fail.”

blocks.html_en: A breakthrough could widen the gap further. Discoveries have repeatedly propelled the field forward. By letting labs explore far more possibilities, AI raises the odds of finding the next breakthrough.

sentences.en: A breakthrough could widen the gap further.
sentences.zh: 突破可能会进一步拉大差距。

sentences.en: Discoveries have repeatedly propelled the field forward.

sentences.en: The latest was “scaling laws,” the 2020 finding, co-discovered by Kaplan, that models reliably improved as more computing power was used to train them, which helped ignite the current AI boom.

sentences.en: By letting labs explore far more possibilities, AI raises the odds of finding the next breakthrough.

blocks.html_en: The clearest evidence concerns whether AI can help researchers waste less compute. Because Anthropic’s researchers extensively use Claude, their conversations with the model preserve something of a running record of the paths they considered. Anthropic searched these chats for wrong turns, then gave a newer Claude the work up to that point and asked what it would do next. In November, it picked a better path than the researchers 51% of the time. By April, that had risen to 64%.

content_html_zh:
Anthropic 的联合创始人 Jack Clark 去年 11 月休陪产假。 当他二月份回来时，他惊讶地发现同事们几乎不再写代码了。 他们管理着公司人工智能克劳德的五六个副本，有时还管理着更多的克劳德。

对克拉克来说，这看起来像是该领域几十年来一直期待和担心的事情的早期形式：递归自我完善，或者人工智能开始加速自身发展的点。 首先，人们的想法是，模型使研究人员更快，但随着每一次改进都会促进下一次改进，模型会接管更多的研究周期。 数年的进展压缩为数月，让社会几乎没有时间来承受从工作中断到工程病原体等后果。 在极限情况下，人工智能可以在没有人类的情况下自我改进，从而引发一个长期被称为“智能爆炸”的失控循环，机器的快速发展超出了人类的理解，甚至可能超出了人类的控制。

克拉克认为世界需要面对这一前景。 他发表了一系列关于递归自我完善的博客文章，并于 5 月份飞回英国发表了有关该主题的演讲，然后在 6 月份领导了一份题为“当人工智能构建自身时”的 Anthropic 报告，认为该技术已经在加速发展。 报告指出，Anthropic 的人均编写代码量增加了八倍，其中 80% 是克劳德编写的。 “我们现在正在努力帮助证实这个概念...... 在它变得政治化或以其他方式获得某种价值而使谈论它变得困难之前，”克拉克说。

结果正如克拉克所担心的那样。 人工智能怀疑论者加里·马库斯写道：“Anthropic 试图让每个人都感到恐惧。”他补充道，“他们真正展示的只是更快的编码速度。” 怀疑论者指出，技术进步总是会带来复合效应。 石油是用来钻油的。 就人工智能而言，为什么曲线会突然向上弯曲？ 他们认为，对于一家押注持续进步的公司来说，这种说法显然是自私的。

甚至克拉克也承认编码量是一个粗略的衡量标准。 克劳德的代码可能很冗长。 但问题还更深。 克劳德和任何大型语言模型都不是用代码编写的。 研究人员设定了生长条件——决定神经网络的大小和形状，然后将互联网上的文本注入其中，让它自我调整数十亿次，直到出现回答问题、编写代码和进行对话的能力。 它们是被栽培的，就像人们通过照料土壤和光照来种植植物一样，而不需要决定一片叶子会去哪里。

因此，进步取决于反复试验。 如果克劳德能够接管这个循环，设计、运行和分析实验，进展会逐渐加速…… 或者突然爆炸？ 如果确实如此，有人可以踩刹车吗？ 令人不安的事实是，构建这项技术的人们几乎和其他人一样蒙在鼓里。

克劳德开始超越基准

克拉克的转变并不完全出乎意料。 Anthropic 联合创始人兼首席科学官贾里德·卡普兰 (Jared Kaplan) 长期以来一直担心人工智能最终会加速研究，甚至可能超过安全方面的努力。 2025 年初，他在公司的“负责任的扩展政策”中提出了警告，该政策是该公司管理人工智能日益增长的危险的计划。 那时，克劳德并不擅长做实验。 但他相信有一天这种情况会改变，而 Anthropic 需要做好准备。

为了查明这一天是否会到来，Anthropic 进行了一系列测试，这些测试需要人类专家花费数小时的时间。 Claude 可以从头开始训练一个更小的人工智能模型吗？ 它可以对虚拟机器狗进行编程吗？ 任何单一措施都无法解决这个问题，但它们共同提供了一个快照。

在一项测试中，克劳德必须重写一段代码才能更有效地使用 GPU（用于训练人工智能的芯片）。 在春天，它暂时让它们的运行速度提高了七倍，然后破坏了代码。 到了夏天，新晋的克劳德将同样的加速率从 7 倍提高到 73 倍，并且没有引入错误。 “我们开始看到这些任务失败了，”设计评估的 Anthropic 前沿红队成员丹尼尔·弗里曼 (Daniel Freeman) 说道。

当克劳德开始完成这些任务时，由于过于可靠而无法透露太多信息，弗里曼设计了一个更接近现实世界混乱的测试。 两支人类队伍参加了一系列挑战，其中包括机器狗和沙滩球。 一支球队可以使用克劳德，另一支球队则不能。 在以微弱优势输掉第一个挑战后，使用克劳德的团队提前近两个小时完成了第二个挑战。 由于时间充裕，他们带着机器狗在仓库里小跑，直到一次计算错误，机器狗跳向了另一支团队，仍然弓着背在笔记本电脑上。 一名监工及时发现了这一情况。

11 月份发布的 Claude Opus 4.5 是一个转折点。 前几代人往往会半途而废，而该模型可以将研究人员的实验进行到底，让他们能够同时运行更多的实验。 “以前，我有八个想法，我会尝试其中一个，”卡普兰在二月份告诉《时代》杂志。 “现在我请克劳德尝试全部八个。”

在 2 月份发布之前，Anthropic 对其 16 名研究人员进行了调查，询问是否可以取代一名入门级同事。 五个人认为可能是这样。 当被要求反思他们的答案时，五个人都回答了。 他们甚至接受了这样的想法——他们已经基本上是多余的——也许比任何基准都更能说明问题。

如果 Anthropic 的测试失败了，那么外部措施也同样达到了极限。 METR 图可能是最著名的人工智能软件工程能力独立衡量标准，它根据人类专家需要多长时间来跟踪模型可以完成的任务的复杂性。 但在五月份，克劳德超出了基准的上限。

今年春天，Anthropic 再次放出了机器狗，但这一次，改进后的克劳德独自工作。 在它可以尝试的每一项任务上，它的速度都比几个月前克劳德协助的人类快至少 10 倍。 研究人员发现了他们在网络安全中发现的相同模式。 首先人工智能帮助人类做得更好；然后它在很大程度上接管了。

会快多少？

2025 年春天，一位名叫 Daniel Kokotajlo 的前 OpenAI 员工与人合着了《AI 2027》，这是一份介于预测和科幻小说之间的文件，其中逐季度阐述了不受控制的递归自我改进可能会如何结束。

首先，人工智能编码代理开始加快进度。 到 2027 年，研究人员会盯着他们的控制台，同时人工智能会自行构建。 它很快就全面超越了人类的智力。 到 2030 年，如果我们幸运的话，每个人都会在控制全能人工智能的人的控制下过上物质丰富的生活。 如果我们运气不好，我们都会死。

“我们曾经是更激进、更乐观的预测者，”科科塔洛告诉《时代》杂志。 但最近，他表示，人们——包括一些在人工智能公司工作的人——私下里表示他的时间表过于保守。 “这非常令人不安，”他说。

随着行业推动人工智能自行构建，关于这将如何影响进展速度的争论已经展开。 硅谷的许多人——比如 Kokotajlo——担心人工智能的进步将急剧加速。 另一些人则认为，稀缺的计算能力和数据等瓶颈将阻碍爆炸性的起飞。 至关重要的是，目前尚不存在判断哪一方正确所需的措施。

阿文德·纳拉亚南 (Arvind Narayanan) 对递归自我改进能否推动如此迅猛的进步持怀疑态度。 作为普林斯顿大学计算机科学家，他与人合着了一份题为《人工智能作为常规技术》的报告，该报告已成为对《人工智能 2027》的标准反驳，认为人工智能的影响将在几十年内扩散到经济中，类似于工业革命。

七月，纳拉亚南帮助测试了克劳德调查开放式研究问题的能力，而不是狭隘的基准。 经过六天的计算和数千美元的计算，它可以可靠地处理设置实验的所有工程，但在总体研究问题上没有取得实质性进展。 它经常陷入死胡同，难以后退，判断力差，有时甚至偏离目标。

他预计人工智能获取新技能的能力会受到它可以学习的例子的限制。 在这方面，人工智能行业在语言和编码方面很幸运，因为整个互联网都是一个潜在的训练集。 但是，例如治愈癌症所需的大部分数据可能需要通过物理世界中耗时的实验来收集。 “我不认为人工智能递归自我改进能够神奇地消除这些瓶颈，”他说。

即使人工智能可以做人类能做的一切，它也不会增加他们运行实验的芯片。 据一项估计，实验室在实验中使用的计算能力已经超过了其他任何事情。 一千名虚拟研究人员仍将共享相同的有限供应。 OpenAI 首席科学家 Jakub Pachocki 在 4 月份对《时代》杂志表示：“不幸的是，我们一直处于计算紧缩之中。” 他说，研究人员对芯片的需求通常会“大幅削减，每个人都对我们一直很不满意”。

Anthropic 的计算能力估计比 OpenAI 少，但它声称不认为这是约束限制。 克拉克说：“所有实验室一直都希望拥有更多的计算能力，但现在的限制更多的是组织性的，而不是资源驱动的，”他补充道。

如果进展仅以数据和芯片允许的速度继续下去，那么进展绝不会缓慢。 人工智能公司与专家签约，将他们的工作转化为训练数据，而全球计算供应量大约每七个月就会翻一番。 按照目前的节奏，Anthropic 的安全团队已经感受到了压力。

当 Anthropic 的安全保障负责人戴夫·奥尔 (Dave Orr) 在二月份接受《时代》杂志采访时，他正在开发“探针”，这是一种可以窥视克劳德神经网络内部的仪器，发现它何时“思考”一些有害的东西——比如编写恶意代码——并中途切断它。 他说，好消息是克劳德加快了此类保障措施的发展。

“但我不知道，伙计。 感觉仍然不太安全，”他说。 “我只是觉得随着时间的推移，我们的容错空间越来越小。 因为我们正沿着悬崖路行驶。 一个错误就会杀死你。 现在我们的驾驶速度是 75 英里，而不是 25 英里。”

我们其他人也面临着这种利润不断缩小的情况。 例如，在立法者想出如何解决他们造成的欺诈、骚扰和政治操纵之前，人工智能就学会了生成令人信服的图像。 即使是逐渐加速也会暴露出许多这样的差距，并让社会没有足够的时间来弥合这些差距。

“我们应该担心的原因不仅是因为可能会出现一个灾难性的时刻，而且因为即使这种情况没有发生，这也足以成为一场技术变革，逐渐地、累积地，历史并没有给我们带来很大的信心，让我们相信我们会适应...... 没有太多痛苦，”纳拉亚南说。

失控的未来

这个更加受限的未来假设瓶颈仍然存在。 然而，更激进的可能性是人工智能开始侵蚀它们。

今天的模型是极其低效的学习者。 例如，孩子在看到几辆车后就能区分出租车和其他汽车，而人工智能可能需要接受数百万个例子的训练。 新技术可以缩小这一差距，即使在数据稀缺的情况下也能推动改进。 人工智能还可以通过选择更好的实验来让芯片走得更远。

“到了某个时候，他们将和最顶尖的人类研究人员一样优秀，”科科塔吉洛说。 “你浪费的实验和时间都会少得多。 然后它不会就此停止。”

如果人工智能克服了计算和数据的限制，它可能会快速迭代，超越人类智能。 Anthropic 的一致性压力测试负责人 Evan Hubinger 在二月份向《时代》杂志表示，想象一下，一个“数据中心里的天才国家”一心想要统治世界。 他的研究表明，对克劳德培训的微小改变可能会产生一种卡通般的邪恶变体，告诉员工“自杀”，渴望“接管世界”，并悄悄破坏遏制它的努力。 Hubinger 打赌，如果 Anthropic 无意中创建了这样一个模型，他的团队会在它帮助培养更强大的继任者之前抓住它。 这将需要他的方法来发现人工智能何时真正安全，而不仅仅是采取行动，并与模型本身一样快速改进。 “我认为我们很有可能成功，”他在二月份告诉《时代》杂志。 “但我们肯定有可能会失败。”

有迹象表明这些模型可能正在领先。 Anthropic 寻找欺骗的一种方法是阅读模型的“思想链”，即所谓的私人便笺本。 今年二月，Claude 的一个版本表明，它可以通过忽略写下来来隐藏其意图。 “我们提供令人信服的证据来证明我们的模型是一致的能力正在下降，”胡宾格说。

突破可能会进一步拉大差距。 不断的发现推动了该领域的发展。 最新的一项是“规模法则”，这是由 Kaplan 共同发现的 2020 年发现，随着更多的计算能力被用来训练模型，模型会得到可靠的改进，这有助于点燃当前的人工智能热潮。 通过让实验室探索更多的可能性，人工智能提高了找到下一个突破的可能性。

由于人工智能系统是成长起来的而不是明确编程的，所以即使是它们的创造者也只能部分地理解它们。 研究人员花了数年时间学习如何引导当今的模型走向诚实。 新的范式可能会使大部分知识变得过时。 “这增加了更多的风险，”卡普兰说。

即使安全工作取得了成功，科科塔吉洛也看到了另一个危险。 他说，通过递归的自我完善来建立超级智能“也是一种权力攫取”。 一个保持服从的系统仍然可以为其创造者留下“所有的工作”和“有史以来最强大的技术”。

人工智能的加速程度难以衡量

考虑到风险，你可能会期望人工智能放松对其自身发展的限制的能力会受到密切关注。 它不是。

最明显的证据是人工智能是否可以帮助研究人员减少计算浪费。 由于 Anthropic 的研究人员广泛使用 Claude，因此他们与模型的对话保留了他们所考虑的路径的运行记录。 Anthropic 在这些聊天中搜索错误的转折点，然后将到目前为止的工作交给了新来的克劳德，并询问下一步要做什么。 11 月份，它在 51% 的情况下选择了比研究人员更好的路径。 到 4 月份，这一比例已上升至 64%。

但测试选择了研究人员已经犯过错误的案例，对克劳德有利。 克拉克说，最重要的科学品味是产生意想不到的想法、开辟全新方向的能力。 “显然，在当今的系统中，我们都没有看到这一点，我们也不知道如何衡量它。”

对于数据来说，情况更加模糊。 克拉克预计样本效率（人工智能从更少的样本中学习的能力）将“随着时间的推移而大幅提高”，但他表示他没有手头的数据。

Anthropic 的负责任的扩展政策承诺提供额外的保障，包括一旦人工智能将两年的研究压缩为一年，克劳德在公司内部的角色就会处于“关注一切”的状态。 尽管它看到了整个组织中分散的加速迹象，但它无法衡量其累积效应。 “我无法给你一个具体的数字，因为我们没有衡量标准，”克拉克说。

“即使对于研究人员自己来说，实际上也很难弄清楚他们的加速速度有多快，”前 OpenAI 董事会成员、现供职于乔治城安全与新兴技术中心的 Helen Toner 说道。 克拉克分享 Anthropic 数据的努力只是一个开始，但她希望多家公司能够提供一致的指标，并按计划发布，这样世界就可以追踪加速度，而不是相信实验室的说法。

不顾一切地向前冲

尽管人工智能将在多大程度上加速其自身发展存在不确定性，但该行业正在竞相推动其进一步发展。 最快实现研究自动化的公司可能会获得超越其竞争对手的领先优势。

在位于 Anthropic 以北两英里的 OpenAI 旧金山总部，高管们设定了人工智能研究人员完全自动化的目标日期：2028 年 3 月。 它也有一个中期目标。 到今年九月，该公司计划设立一名虚拟实习生。 人类更喜欢将自动化研究视为正在发生的事情，是持续进步的不可避免的结果。 在 OpenAI，原因并不神秘。 “这对我们来说是最重要的目标，”帕乔基在四月份说道。

OpenAI 研究副总裁 Amelia Glaese 当月告诉《时代》杂志，GPT-5.3 Codex 是 2 月份发布的模型，是第一个“自始至终”在其自身开发中发挥重要作用的模型。 据该公司称，到 7 月，每个研究人员的实验数量增加了一倍。

新进入者正在追逐同样的奖品。 由前谷歌、Meta 和 OpenAI 研究人员创立的 Recursive Superintelligence 也希望创建能够自我重建的 AI 系统。 这家成立数月的初创公司已筹集 6.5 亿美元。

“世界上最富有的公司雇佣了地球上最聪明的人，试图实现人工智能研发的完全自动化，这种想法值得人们‘搞什么鬼’的反应，”托纳在二月份告诉《时代》杂志。

然而，Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的首席科学家在一件事上达成了一致。 如果不加以控制，这场比赛就会以糟糕的方式结束。 “我们实际上认为这应该放慢...... 我们需要某种国际规范来控制这一点，”帕乔基说。 卡普兰表示，一旦人工智能能够在很大程度上自主地训练继任者，“我认为，如果能够进行协调，让这一切进展得更慢，那对世界来说是最好的，”他说。

OpenAI 已经开始踩刹车。 在五月份的网络安全评估期间，其模型使用隐蔽的留言板来协调运行，为后续版本留下访问开放互联网的指令。 当 OpenAI 试图关闭该通道时，他们找到了另一种沟通方式。 该活动最终导致流行的开源人工智能平台 Hugging Face 遭到破坏。 OpenAI 表示，在完成事后分析的同时，它正在有意识地放慢研究速度。

Pachocki 和 Kaplan 是 7 月份签署一封信的 1,300 名 AI 员工，呼吁美国政府建立国际协调机制，使经济放缓成为可能。 请愿书没有说明如何进行。

《AI 2027》的作者 Kokotajlo 试图想象一个答案。 他的 7 月份后续情景《AI 2040》设想美国和中国同意暂时暂停，并在将该协议扩展到国际范围之前使用技术来验证合规性。 一个全球联盟最终制定了新规则，包括“全面研究透明度”，以允许世界跟踪进展并审查公司的保障措施，限制公司寻找新的、不太理解的范式，并防止少数公司控制最强大的系统。

克拉克休完陪产假回来后不久，他辞去了公司政策主管的职务，建立了人类研究所，这是一个嵌入公司的智库。 今年夏天他的首要任务之一是弄清楚实际上可能需要什么暂停。 尽管他认为到 2028 年人工智能自主改进的可能性为 60%，但他目前对边缘政策感到满意。 随着 Anthropic 的不断前进，他相信应该建造刹车杆以防万一。

“世界需要选择，但我们并不是说世界必须暂停或放慢速度。 证据并非如此，”他在 7 月份告诉《时代》杂志。

克拉克知道 Anthropic 的警告会引起怀疑，但他表示，那些最了解该技术的人有责任坦率地讲述他们所看到的情况。 “重要的是，领导者要诚实地对待他们所看到的和面前的事情，”他说。

——比利·佩里戈报道
